content.thinking:
I'm checking the root cause claims against the cited sources. Request volume rose well above the earlier level, but the CPU available to serve it stayed fixed at the replica limits, and that matches the stated 3.0-core ceiling. CPU then hit that ceiling at full utilization, so requests queued and response times stretched.

I'm checking whether the contributing-factor claim about replicas holds up. The record shows three replicas at one point after load rose and a scale-out that started from three, but it doesn't show the replica count across the whole window, so I can't confirm it stayed at three throughout.

I'm checking whether the contributing-factor claim about the Code-Fix reading is accurate. The record says it re-added every purchase up to that one, which is narrower than the "whole purchase history each time" wording I'm looking at, so that phrasing may overstate what was found. The rest of that entry is supported.

I'm checking the "whole history" wording against Code-Fix's actual finding, which was narrower: it re-added each purchase up to that one, so that phrasing may overstate it. The rest of that entry holds up. Nobody was paged and no on-call incident is linked, which the record supports. The action items aren't something I'm judging here, and I'm treating the "still at risk" point as a conditional supported by the rise in volume, the fixed CPU ceiling, and the fix not yet merged.

flags.quote: According to Code-Fix's reading of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, the account page's default path (when neither rollout flag is set) likely re-adds a shopper's whole purchase history once for every purchase on each render.
flags.why: Code-Fix says the loop re-adds the purchases up to each one (a growing prefix, n(n+1)/2 reads), not the whole history once per purchase.

supported.quote: Request volume to io-shop rose well above its earlier level while the service ran on a fixed amount of CPU ({T7.2} replicas, each under a CPU limit, as of T7). CPU use climbed to that limit, so requests had to wait for CPU and response times stretched.
rows: The series behind the alert ... 214.76666666666668 ms before it began, 1316.5 ms on average while it was broken

supported.quote: Far more requests than usual reached the shop and used up the fixed amount of computing power its servers had, so requests had to wait their turn; the shop's account page likely also does much more work per request than it needs to, which made that limit come sooner.
Another rise in request volume could use up the service's CPU again and slow its responses the same way.

rows: The series behind the alert ... 1316.5 ms on average while it was broken, and 1803 ms at its worst

supported.quote: People using the shop waited much longer for responses: from the onset, the response time that nearly all requests stay under climbed far above its usual level, and the latency alert fired.
rows: The series behind the alert ... 214.76666666666668 ms before it began, 1316.5 ms on average while it was broken

supported.quote: Requests were waiting for CPU: the service's CPU use rose to the limit set for it and stayed close to that limit while the service was broken.
The CPU filled up because request volume climbed far above its earlier level. Nothing about the service changed: the change that set the incident off was the rise in load.
rows: The record confirmed [C1]: the load outgrew the CPU the service had

supported.quote: The higher volume outgrew the fixed CPU that the service's {T7.2} replicas had as of T7.
The service did not add replicas as load grew. It stayed at {T7.2} replicas (as of T7) until the Mitigation Agent scaled it out by hand. No autoscaling of io-shop was seen in the record.
That would make each request cost far more CPU than its answer needs. Nothing ran this reading.
rows: What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed ... nothing ran its test or its fix

supported.quote: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was brought in when it fired.
rows: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.
